desc:
You are given a binary search tree and a list of queries. Each query is a pair [lo, hi]. For every query, count how many values x in the tree satisfy lo ≤ x ≤ hi, and return the counts in the order of the queries.

There can be many queries, so a full traversal per query is too slow; answer each one in roughly O(h) time.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [5,2,7,-1,3,6] is the tree whose root 5 has left child 2 and right child 7; node 2 has no left child and right child 3; node 7 has left child 6 and no right child.

Example

tree = [8,4,12,2,6,10,14], queries = [[3,9],[0,100],[15,20],[8,8]]
Output: [3,7,0,1]
The values are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Between 3 and 9 there are 4, 6 and 8.
constraints: 0 ≤ node value ≤ 100,000, all values distinct; the tree is a valid BST
hints: Walking the whole tree for every query costs O(n) each. The answer to a range query can be built from two simpler questions.
Define rank(x) = how many values are strictly smaller than x. Then the answer is rank(hi + 1) - rank(lo).
Store the subtree size at every node. To compute rank(x), descend from the root: when you go right at a node, add 1 + size of its left subtree; when you go left, add nothing.
editorial: Compute the size of every subtree once. Nodes are numbered in level order, so processing them from the last to the first guarantees that both children are done before their parent. Then rank(x), the count of values strictly below x, is found by a single root-to-leaf walk: at a node with value v, if v < x then the node and its entire left subtree are smaller than x, so add 1 + size[left] and go right; otherwise go left.

A range [lo, hi] contains rank(hi + 1) - rank(lo) values (values are integers). Each query costs O(h), so the total is O(n + q · h). Flattening the tree into a sorted array and using two binary searches is an equivalent alternative with O(n) memory.
